subject: Biology
title: Food Chains
description: A quick win: understand Food Chains.

hook.text: Energy moves through an ecosystem in a straight line: sun to plant to herbivore to predator.

buildup.text: Each link is called a trophic level. Producers sit at the bottom, top predators at the peak.

discovery.text: Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next. The rest is lost as heat.

twist.text: That's why top predators are rare—there's barely enough energy left to support them.

climax.text: If toxins enter the chain, they concentrate upward. Predators get the highest doses.

punchline.text: Energy shrinks at every step up the chain.

quiz.question: About how much energy passes from one trophic level to the next?

details.summary: A food chain traces the linear path of energy from producers to consumers in an ecosystem. Energy flows from photosynthetic organisms to herbivores, then to predators, with roughly 90 percent lost as heat at each trophic level, limiting chain length to four or five links.
details.whyItMatters: Food chains illustrate the fundamental energy flow through ecosystems and explain why top predators are always rare. Understanding energy transfer efficiency is essential for managing fisheries, agriculture, and conservation.
takeaways: Energy transfers between trophic levels are only about 10 percent efficient
Most food chains have four or five links due to energy loss
Removing any link can collapse the chain above it

faq.question: Why are there so few top predators in any ecosystem?
faq.answer: Only about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. By the time energy reaches top predators, very little remains. This energy limitation means ecosystems can support far fewer predators than herbivores or producers.

faq.question: What happens when a link in a food chain disappears?
faq.answer: If a prey species disappears, predators above must find alternatives or decline. If a predator disappears, prey populations can explode, overgrazing their food supply and causing cascading effects down the chain. This is called a trophic cascade.
